summary: This specification defines a profile for issuing OAuth 2.0 access tokens in JSON Web Token (JWT) format. Authorization servers and resource servers from different vendors can follow it to issue and consume access tokens in an interoperable manner.

eli5.summary: An access token is like a ticket that lets you into a ride. This document says exactly how to write the ticket in a standard format, so rides made by different companies can all read it.

subtitle: A standard layout for OAuth 2.0 access tokens issued as JWTs, so servers from different vendors can issue and check them the same way.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 does not mandate a format for access tokens. Many vendors issued JWT access tokens with the same general layout but different claim names and syntax, which hurt interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The profile requires signed JWTs with the typ header value at+jwt, a fixed set of required claims (iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat, jti), and lists the checks a resource server MUST make before accepting one.
tldr.outcome: Authorization servers and resource servers from different vendors can issue and consume JWT access tokens in an interoperable manner, with security and privacy pitfalls spelled out.

facts.label: Required claims
facts.value: iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat, jti

today: RFC 9068 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a JWT Access Token Profile
sections.content:
The OAuth 2.0 framework (RFC 6749) does not mandate any format for access tokens. In practice, many commercial implementations issue tokens that a resource server can parse and validate directly, without asking the authorization server. This is common when the two are run by different entities or separated by some boundary, and many use the JSON Web Token (JWT) format (RFC 7519).

Those vendor tokens share a similar layout, and the differences are mostly the claim names and syntax. This profile standardizes a common set of claims and validation rules, tells authorization servers how request parameters shape the token, and tells resource servers how to validate it. It also gives security and privacy guidance against naive use of JWTs as access tokens.

It is not the same as RFC 7523, which defines how a JWT can be used to request an access token. This document defines how to encode access tokens as JWTs.
sections.eli5: Many shops already made their own tickets that looked almost alike but used different words. This document picks one set of words so every ride can read every ticket.

sections.title: The Token Header
sections.content:
JWT access tokens MUST be signed, and MUST NOT use none as the signing algorithm. Any signing algorithm may be used, but asymmetric cryptography is RECOMMENDED because it makes it easier for resource servers to get validation information. Servers following the profile MUST include RS256 among their supported signature algorithms.

The profile registers the application/at+jwt media type. Tokens MUST carry it in the typ header parameter, and because RFC 7515 recommends omitting the application/ prefix, the value SHOULD be at+jwt. This explicit typing helps keep OpenID Connect ID Tokens from being accepted as access tokens.
sections.eli5: The ticket must have an unforgeable stamp and a label saying "this is a ride ticket, not a library card".

sections.title: The Claims
sections.content:
Seven claims are REQUIRED: iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti. For sub, the value SHOULD identify the resource owner when a resource owner is involved (for example the authorization code grant), and SHOULD identify the client application when none is (for example the client credentials grant).

Authentication information claims auth_time, acr and amr are OPTIONAL, defined in OpenID Connect Core. Additional identity attributes SHOULD use the claim name from the IANA JWT registry. Other attributes are allowed if the claim names are collision resistant or the tokens are for a private subsystem.

If the authorization request had a scope parameter, the token SHOULD include a scope claim, and every scope string MUST have meaning for the resources in aud. For roles, groups and entitlements, servers SHOULD use the groups, roles and entitlements attributes of the SCIM User schema from RFC 7643, which this document registers as JWT claims.
sections.eli5: The ticket lists who made it, who it is for, who holds it, and when it runs out. Extra lines such as seat number are optional.

sections.title: Requesting and Issuing a Token
sections.content:
An authorization server can issue a JWT access token for any grant defined by RFC 6749 and its extensions. If the request has a resource parameter (RFC 8707), the aud claim SHOULD have the same value. If it does not, the server MUST use a default resource indicator in aud, and SHOULD infer it from scope when that is present. If the scopes point to different default resources, the server SHOULD reject the request with invalid_scope.

The server MUST NOT issue a JWT access token if the authorization it grants would be ambiguous. The RFC's example shows an authorization code request with resource and scope parameters, and the token that results, with typ at+JWT and algorithm RS256.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a ticket, you can say which ride it is for. If you do not, the booth picks the ride it thinks you mean, and refuses if it cannot tell.

sections.title: Validating a Token
sections.content:
Authorization servers SHOULD advertise their signing keys through jwks_uri and the expected iss through the issuer value using Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414). An OpenID Connect server MAY use its discovery document instead, and if it supports both, the values MUST be consistent.

A resource server receiving a token MUST check that:

  • the typ header is at+jwt or application/at+jwt, and reject any other value;
  • if the token is encrypted, it is decrypted with the keys the resource server specified at registration (and an unencrypted token SHOULD be rejected if encryption was negotiated);
  • the iss claim exactly matches the issuer identifier;
  • the aud claim contains a resource indicator the resource server expects for itself;
  • the signature is valid using the alg header, which MUST NOT be none, and the keys provided by the authorization server;
  • the current time is before exp, with at most a small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, for clock skew.

On any failure the response MUST include the error code invalid_token, as in RFC 6750. If the token has authorization claims, the resource server SHOULD combine them with other contextual information to decide whether to allow the call.
sections.eli5: The ride attendant checks that the ticket has the right label, is for this ride, has a real stamp and has not run out. If anything is off, the ticket is refused.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Because the token layout resembles an OpenID Connect ID token, the required explicit typing, in line with RFC 8725, helps the resource server tell them apart. To prevent cross-JWT confusion, authorization servers MUST use a distinct aud value for tokens issued by the same issuer for distinct resources. Servers should also stop clients from influencing sub in confusing ways, for example by registering an arbitrary client_id that matches a high-privilege resource owner.

Using different keys for ID tokens and access tokens does not limit damage from a leaked key, since resource servers cannot know which key to expect and must accept any published key.

On privacy, tokens carry information by value, so clients and possibly end users can read unencrypted claims. The client MUST NOT inspect the content of the access token, because the format may change at any time, for example to opaque tokens. Measures to limit leakage include encrypting the token or sensitive claims, omitting them, or falling back on opaque tokens. Since sub is mandatory, resource servers can correlate requests. To prevent that, the server can give different resource servers different sub values, or even a different sub for every token.
sections.eli5: Do not let someone reuse a library card as a ride ticket, and remember that anyone holding the ticket may be able to read what is written on it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registration covers two things. The first is the media type application/at+jwt in the Media Types registry, for content that is an access token encoded as a JWT, with intended usage COMMON and the IETF as change controller. The second is the claim names roles, groups and entitlements in the JSON Web Token (JWT) registry, pointing at RFC 7643 and Section 2.2.3.1 of this document.
sections.eli5: The new ticket label and three new ticket line names are written in the official list so nobody else reuses them.

viz.caption: REQUIRED CLAIMS IN A JWT ACCESS TOKEN

items.label: Expiration time
items.desc: The token must be rejected at or after this time.

items.label: Audience
items.desc: The resource the token is for.

items.label: Subject
items.desc: The resource owner, or the client when there is no resource owner.
